extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in mass communication/media studies
extracted.subtask_description: Frameworks and practical criteria for analyzing mass media content (news and entertainment) using quantitative and qualitative methods, including what to measure (frequency, prominence, representation, visual/verbal techniques) and theoretical stances (humanistic vs behaviorist; media as channel vs participant).

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat news and entertainment as a unified symbolic environment
rubrics_metrics.description: News and entertainment both tell us something about the world, and together they make up a significant symbolic environment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss content labeled 'entertainment' as less culturally potent; both types convey who is important, how to behave, and what trends are. Analyses should include both news and entertainment when assessing media's symbolic environment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure frequency/presence of items
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzing how frequently things, people, and places appear in media content is valuable because 'the more frequently a given stimulus is found, the more potent is its presumed effect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantify occurrences to summarize patterns and enable comparison to reality benchmarks (e.g., percent of Latinos shown vs percent in population). Frequency counts are central to many social-science content analyses but do not capture full contextual meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare content to external reality benchmarks
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyzing frequency allows comparison of media content to some reality benchmark (e.g., the percentage of Latinos shown on prime-time television versus the percentage of Latinos in the total U.S. population).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose an appropriate, defensible benchmark when asserting distortion or bias; without a suitable reference standard, claims of bias are weak.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on systematic, repetitive, organizationally-produced patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Researchers are drawn to repetitive patterns of widely attended mediated messages that were produced by media organizations in a routine and standardized way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize systematic patterns over idiosyncratic items; these routine practices are most likely to reveal underlying cultural or organizational logics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adopt and state analytic tradition (humanistic v. behaviorist)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humanists examine content for aesthetic meanings and internal logic; behaviorists examine content as stimuli that produce effects and tend to quantify content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit whether the study treats content as 'text' worthy of interpretive analysis (qualitative/rhetorical) or as an observable set of stimuli whose frequency and attributes predict audience effects (quantitative). Choose methods consistent with the theoretical stance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative v. qualitative method choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Behavioral content analysis tends toward quantitative techniques; humanistic approaches gravitate toward qualitative analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize tradeoffs: quantification summarises what is present and allows comparisons, but may miss contextual meanings and codes; qualitative analysis captures meanings but is less easily generalizable or comparable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the content analysis standard: objective, systematic, quantitative, manifest
rubrics_metrics.description: Content analysis defined as the 'objective, systematic, quantitative and manifest analysis of content' (Berelson, 1952).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When doing content analysis, strive for operational definitions, consistent coding rules, and manifest indicators that can be reliably measured. Note limitations in capturing latent or contextual meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide theoretical stance on media role (passive channel v. active participant)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some models treat media as passive transmitters of events (channels); others view media as actively manipulating or constructing reality (participants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chosen stance shapes interpretation: a 'channel' model focuses on source/audience factors and selection among existing messages; an 'active' model examines how media structure, emphasize, relocate, label, and otherwise manipulate events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examine selection, evaluation, and interpretation devices (journalistic correlation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalistic correlation defined as 'selection, evaluation and interpretation of events' and signifies the relative importance of what is reported through headlines and other devices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code and analyze devices such as headlines, leads, placement, and editorial conventions that signal importance and frame events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess prominence and allocation of attention
rubrics_metrics.description: One way media structure the symbolic environment is by giving greater attention (in the form of more time, greater prominence, etc.) to certain events, people, groups, and places than others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure time, column inches, placement, and prominence as indicators of salience; prominence often correlates with perceived importance irrespective of objective event frequency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Code representational characteristics (who appears and how)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine whom the media show: personal characteristics, social origins, where they come from in the social system, behaviors exhibited, and presentation relative to others in society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include demographic attributes, institutional roles, behavior types, and relational framing (acting vs acted upon) in coding schemes to reveal representational patterns and possible stereotyping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look for manipulation techniques (selection, labeling, stereotyping, relocation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Media single out and highlight certain elements over others; they can impose logic via emphasis, stereotyping, relocation of events/people, and rhetorical labels (e.g., 'freedom fighter' vs 'terrorist').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Code not only presence but framing choices: labels, metaphors, story selection, and what is left out. Use examples (photo selection/cropping, juxtaposition, choice of camera angles) to illustrate manipulative mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include visual-analysis criteria (camera perspective, cropping, shot selection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pictures can be distorted by cropping, angles, and shot selection; camera perspectives can manipulate perception (e.g., eye-level vs low/high angle shots).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing televised or photographed content, include coding categories for shot type, camera angle, framing, cropping, and montage/juxtaposition. Do not assume pictures are transparent representations of reality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply McQuail's typology of news bias (open/hidden × intended/unintended)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bias can be categorized by whether it is open or hidden and intended or unintended, producing: partisanship (open/intended), propaganda (hidden/intended), unwitting bias (open/unintended), and ideology (hidden/unintended).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this typology to classify bias evidence: partisanship includes explicit endorsements; propaganda is intentionally partisan but disguised (e.g., PR/disinformation); unwitting bias includes topic selection; ideology denotes embedded hidden assumptions in texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate benchmarks and be cautious about simple quantitative balance
rubrics_metrics.description: A convincing case of bias requires an acceptable standard of fairness; quantitative balance (e.g., equal seconds or column inches) is not always a good standard because events do not occur in balanced amounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justify the benchmark used for comparisons (events-driven vs equality of space/time) and consider event occurrence and newsworthiness when interpreting counts. Beware misinterpreting imbalance that reflects real differences in events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample major mass media and widely shared content
rubrics_metrics.description: Content research traditionally focuses on mediated content that is widely shared by a large audience—major mass media such as television, newspapers, and magazines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For studies of social impact, prioritize sampling channels with wide audience reach; explicitly state exclusions (e.g., memos, cassette recordings, books) and rationale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish symbolic/horse-race coverage from issue-oriented coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: News often conveys 'who is ahead' (horse race/symbolic coverage) rather than substantive issue orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate stories that function as symbolic signaling (campaign momentum, symbolic events) from those focused on policy substance; code story orientation to detect prevalence of 'symbolic' versus 'issue' reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate cross-channel discrepancies
rubrics_metrics.description: Different media channels can provide radically different views of the same world; researchers should examine the extent to which channels impose their own structure and logic on events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare coverage of the same event across multiple outlets/channels to detect framing differences, omissions, and divergent emphases; use parallel coding schemes for comparability.
